en: The Sūtra of the Benevolent Kings’ Prajñāpāramitā, Volume One, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin Dynasty.
Chapter One: The Introduction. Introduction. First.
Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was dwelling on Vulture Peak Mountain in the city of Rājagṛha, together with a great assembly of eight hundred billion bhikṣus—both those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), all of whom were arhats. They had fully accomplished conditioned and unconditioned merits; the ten knowledges of those beyond training, the eight knowledges of those in training, and the six knowledges of those in training; the three faculties and the sixteen mental applications; the contemplations on the emptiness of phenomena, the emptiness of sensations, and the emptiness of names; the three gates of emptiness; the Four Noble Truths and the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination; and they had achieved immeasurable virtues.

Furthermore, there were eight hundred trillion great seers and pratyekabuddhas who were neither subject to annihilation nor eternalism, having fully accomplished the Four Noble Truths and the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination.

There were also nine million trillion bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, all of whom possessed the merit of the true wisdom of arhats and the merit of the wisdom of skillful means; they practiced the Mahāyāna alone and had fully accomplished the four eyes, the five supernormal powers, the three types of penetration, the ten powers, the four immeasurable minds, the four analytical knowledges, the four means of integration, and the adamantine meditative absorption. All such merits were perfected in them.

Furthermore, there were thousands of millions of virtuous ones who had observed the five precepts; they all practiced the ten stages of an arhat, dedicated themselves toward the fulfillment of the fivefold dharma-body, and had fully accomplished immeasurable merits.

Furthermore, there were ten thousand laywomen who had received the five precepts and possessed pure faith; all of them practiced the ten stages of an arhat and had fully accomplished the merit of initial birth, the merit of abiding birth, and the merit of final birth—thus accomplishing the merit of all thirty births.
Furthermore, there were ten billion virtuous lay practitioners (*gṛhapati*) who were fully endowed with moral conduct:

they had perfected the twenty-two factors, the ten totalities (*kṛtsnāyatana*), the eight bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), the eight liberations (*vimokṣa*), the three types of wisdom, the sixteen truths, the four truths, and the contemplations of the four, three, two, and one stages; they had attained the ninety-fold patience, and all their meritorious qualities were fully accomplished.

Furthermore, there were ten million billion Brahmās of the Nine, the Three Pure, the Three Radiant, the Three Brahma, and the Five Joyful Heavens; they possessed the meditative concentrations of the heavens, the concentration of merit, the savoring of flavors, and the constant joy of supernormal powers, having fully accomplished the merits of the eighteen places of rebirth.

Furthermore, there were billions upon billions of sons of the gods from the six heavens of the desire realm, who had all achieved the fruits of the ten wholesome actions as well as supernatural powers and meritorious virtues.

There were also sixteen great kings, each with a retinue of ten thousand, twenty thousand, or even up to one hundred thousand, who were fully endowed with the merit of the five precepts, the ten wholesome actions, and the three refuges, and who practiced the conduct of pure faith.
Furthermore, there were all sentient beings of the five paths;
furthermore, there were immeasurable multitudes from other directions;

furthermore, the pure lands of the ten directions were transformed, manifesting ten billion high seats and emanating ten billion Sumeru-like precious lotuses, each with a transformed Buddha seated upon the lotus before them, along with immeasurable transformation Buddhas.

There were immeasurable bodhisattvas, bhikṣus, and the eightfold assembly, each seated upon a precious lotus flower. Upon each flower were immeasurable lands; in every one of these lands, the Buddhas and their assemblies were no different from those present here now.
Within each and every land, each Buddha and their respective great assemblies each preached the Prajñāpāramitā.

The great assemblies from other directions, the transformed assemblies, the great assemblies within these three realms, and the twelve great assemblies all came to gather together and sat upon lotus thrones that endure for nine kalpas.
The assembly was square and vast, spanning nine hundred and fifty *li*, with the great multitude seated in solemn harmony.

At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha—the one endowed with the ten titles and the three types of clear knowledge, who has realized the Great Truth of Cessation through Vajra-Wisdom—on the eighth day of the first month, having just ascended to the tenth stage (*bhūmi*), entered the Samādhi of the Great Chamber of Quiescence. Contemplating conditions, he emitted a great radiance that illuminated the triple world.

Furthermore, from the crown of his head there emerged a thousand-jeweled lotus flower; this flower extended upward as far as the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-Perception, and its light likewise reached as far as the Buddha-lands of other directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

At that time, from the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), immeasurable transformations of great fragrant flowers rained down; their fragrance was like chariot wheels and the flowers were like Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains, descending like clouds.
The eighteen Brahmā kings rained down flowers of a hundred different colors;
the gods of the six heavens of desire (*ṣaḍ kāmāvacarā devāḥ*) rained down flowers of immeasurable colors.

Before that Buddha’s seat, nine hundred million *koṭi* of lotuses—according to the old edition, "tiers" (*jì*)—spontaneously arose, reaching upward as far as the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-Perception; at that time, the earth of this world shook in six ways.
At that time, the entire great assembly was simultaneously struck with doubt and said to one another:

"The World-Honored One, the Greatly Awakened One, who possesses the four fearlessnesses, the eighteen unique qualities, and the dharma-body of the five eyes, has previously, for the sake of us, the great assembly, expounded the Mahāprajñāpāramitā, the Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā, the Rājan-paripṛcchā-prajñāpāramitā, and the Prajñāpāramitā-ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā over the course of twenty-nine years."
"Today the Tathāgata has emitted a great radiance; what purpose does this serve?

At that time, among the sixteen great kings, King Prasenajit of Śrāvastī—known as Candraprabha—whose virtue reached the ten stages and who practiced the six perfections, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, and the four kinds of unshakable faith, was engaged in the transformation of the Mahāyāna. He successively questioned eight hundred people, including the layman Ratnacchattra and Vimalakīrti;
he further questioned five thousand people, including Subhūti and Śāriputra.
He further questioned Maitreya, Siṃhanāda, and ten thousand others, yet none were able to answer.

At that time, King Prasenajit immediately employed his supernormal powers to produce eighty thousand kinds of music; the eighteen Brahma-heavens and the various devas of the six desire realms likewise produced eighty thousand kinds of music. The sound vibrated through the three-thousandfold world system and even reached the Buddha-lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the ten directions, manifesting wherever there were those with whom it had a karmic connection.

From that Buddha-land in another direction, the Bodhisattva Southern Dharma-talent (Dakṣiṇā-dharmamati) arrived together with a great assembly of five hundred million billion beings to enter this grand gathering;
from the east, the Bodhisattva Jewel-Pillar (Ratnastaṃbha) arrived together with a great assembly of nine hundred million billion beings to enter this grand gathering;
from the north, the Bodhisattva Nature-of-Space (Gaganasvabhāva) arrived together with a great assembly of one hundred thousand million billion beings to enter this grand gathering.
From the western direction, the Bodhisattva Supratiṣṭhita, together with a great assembly as numerous as ten Ganges Rivers, arrived at this great gathering.
It was the same in the other six directions; they likewise performed music and produced immeasurable musical sounds to awaken the Tathāgata.
The Buddha, knowing the time had come and perceiving the faculties of the assembly, arose from meditative concentration and sat upon a lotus lion throne like a king of vajra mountains.
The great assembly rejoiced, each manifesting immeasurable supernatural powers, as the multitude remained upon the earth and in the sky.

Chapter Two: Contemplating Emptiness (*Śūnyatā-vipaśyanā-parivarta*) from the *Benevolent Kings’ Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra for the Protection of the State*. At that time, the Buddha addressed the great assembly:
"I know that the sixteen great kings intend to inquire about the causes and conditions for protecting their kingdoms."
I shall now first explain for all the bodhisattvas the causes and conditions for protecting the fruit of Buddhahood, and the causes and conditions for protecting the practices of the ten stages.
Listen attentively, listen attentively!
Reflect upon this well and practice in accordance with the Dharma!
Then King Prasenajit said:
"Excellent!
It is for the sake of a great causal connection!"
He immediately scattered flowers of a hundred billion colors, which transformed into a hundred billion jeweled canopies, covering the entire great assembly.
At that time, the Great King rose again, paid homage, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"How do all bodhisattvas protect the fruit of Buddhahood?
How do they protect the causes and conditions for the practices of the ten stages?
The Buddha said:

“The Bodhisattva transforms the four modes of birth, yet does not contemplate the suchness of form, nor the suchness of sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; the suchness of sentient beings, self, person, permanence, bliss, selfhood, or purity; the suchness of the knower, the viewer, or the life-principle; the suchness of the Bodhisattva; the suchness of the six perfections, the four means of integration, and all practices; and the suchness of the two truths.”

Therefore, the true nature of all phenomena is emptiness: it neither comes nor goes, is without arising or ceasing, is identical to the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), equal to the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), non-dual, undifferentiated, and like space.

"Therefore, the aggregates, sense bases, and elements are without self and lack any marks of existence; this is the Bodhisattva’s practice of transformation through the *prajñāpāramitā* of the ten stages.
He addressed the Buddha, saying, "If all dharmas are thus, when a Bodhisattva protects and transforms sentient beings, is it for the sake of transforming sentient beings?"
“Great King!

The nature of dharmas (dharmatā) is that form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are permanent, blissful, self, and pure. They do not abide in form, nor do they abide in non-form, nor do they abide in that which is neither form nor non-form; this applies even to sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, which likewise do not abide in that which is neither abiding nor non-abiding.”
Why is this? It is not the suchness of form, nor is it the non-suchness of form.

Because of conventional truth and because of the three provisional designations, one speaks of "seeing sentient beings. Since the nature of all beings is real, even the Buddhas, the Three Vehicles, the seven types of worthies, and the eight types of noble ones are called "seeing," and even the sixty-two views are called "seeing."
"Great King!
If one views all phenomena by means of names—even including the Buddhas, the three vehicles, and the four modes of birth—this is not a case of not viewing all phenomena."
He addressed the Buddha, saying:
“The Prajñāpāramitā possesses dharmas that are not non-dharmas; how does the Mahāyāna illuminate them?
“Great King! [the Buddha replied.]
In the Mahāyāna, one does not perceive phenomena as being non-phenomena; if phenomena are not non-phenomena, this is called the emptiness of non-non-phenomena.

The nature of phenomena is empty; form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty; the twelve bases, the eighteen elements, and the six great elements are empty; and the Four Noble Truths and the twelve links of dependent origination are empty.
This dharma arises, abides, and ceases simultaneously; it is both existent and empty. In every single moment, it is likewise a dharma that arises, abides, and ceases. Why is this?

Ninety kṣaṇas constitute one thought-moment (citta-kṣaṇa); within one thought-moment, a single kṣaṇa undergoes nine hundred births and cessations. This applies likewise to all phenomena, including form (rūpa).

Because the *prajñāpāramitā* is empty, one does not perceive conditions, nor does one perceive the truths; indeed, all dharmas are empty: internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, beginningless emptiness, essential emptiness, ultimate emptiness, the emptiness of *prajñāpāramitā*, the emptiness of causes, the emptiness of the fruit of Buddhahood, and even the emptiness of emptiness itself.

It exists because of the accumulation of phenomena; it exists because of the accumulation of sensation; it exists because of the accumulation of names; it exists because of the accumulation of causes; it exists because of the accumulation of effects; it exists because of the ten practices; it exists because of the fruit of Buddhahood; and so on, up to the existence of all things within the six realms.
"Good son!
If there is a bodhisattva who perceives dharmas, sentient beings, self, person, or cognitive views, such a person, though walking in the world, is no different from those of the world."

Regarding all phenomena, there is no movement, no arrival, and no cessation; there is neither mark nor absence of mark. All phenomena are suchness (*tathatā*); the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha are also suchness. This is precisely the single thought-moment of the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*), which fully possesses the eighty-four thousand *prajñāpāramitās*. It is designated as the Mahāyāna; it is the extinction that is the diamond (*vajra*); it is also called concentration (*samādhi*), and it is also called all practices (*sarvacaryā*).
As it is said in the *Prasphullitapadma-prajñāpāramitā*: "Great King!
The names, phrases, and syllables of this sutra are the names, phrases, and syllables spoken by a hundred Buddhas, a thousand Buddhas, and hundreds of thousands of millions of Buddhas."

If one were to fill as many trichiliocosm world-systems as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River with immeasurable seven treasures and bestow them upon the sentient beings within those trichiliocosms, such that they all attained the seven stages of worthiness and the four fruits of arhatship, it would not equal the merit of giving rise to a single thought of faith in this sutra, let alone understanding a single phrase!
Because phrases, non-phrases, and non-non-phrases do not exist, Prajñā is not a phrase, a phrase is not Prajñā, and Prajñā is also not a Bodhisattva. Why is this?

Because the three births within each of the ten stages are empty; the birth at the beginning, the birth during the stay, and the birth at the end cannot be apprehended, for the three births within each stage are empty.
Nor is it omniscience (sarvajñā), nor is it the Mahāyāna, because they are empty.
"Great King!

If a bodhisattva perceives objects, perceives cognition, perceives the teaching, or perceives a recipient, this is not the noble vision; it is the perception of phenomena through inverted conceptualization, the way of an ordinary person."
That which is seen as the three realms is a designation for the karmic retribution of sentient beings.
When the six consciousnesses give rise to immeasurable and inexhaustible desires, it is called the "emptiness of the treasury of the desire realm.
Alternatively, when karma and its fruits arise from form, it is called the "emptiness of the treasury of the form realm."
Or, the karmic fruits arising from mental factors are called the "empty treasury of the formless realm.

The three realms are empty; the fundamental ignorance that is the treasury of the three realms is also empty. Regarding the nine cycles of birth and extinction across the three stages, the remaining habitual tendencies of ignorance and their retributive fruits within the first three realms are empty.

Because the Bodhisattva Vajra has attained the Samādhi of the Exhaustion of Principles, whether it be the emptiness of the arising and ceasing of effects, the emptiness of having effects, the emptiness due to the emptiness of causes, or even the emptiness of *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge), all are empty.
The emptiness of the fruit of cessation: because it was already empty previously, the Buddha attains the three unconditioned fruits.
These are the emptinesses of the emptiness of cessation through wisdom, the emptiness of cessation not through wisdom, and the emptiness of the fruit of *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge) and space.
"Good son!

If there is one who practices listening and speaking, yet there is neither listening nor speaking, being like empty space; when dharmas are identical to the dharma-nature, listening is identical to speaking, and all dharmas are thusness."
Great King!
Such is the manner in which a bodhisattva cultivates the protection of the fruit of Buddhahood.

To protect the *prajñāpāramitā* is to protect omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), the ten powers, the eighteen unique qualities, the five eyes, the fivefold dharma-body, the four immeasurable minds, and all fruits of merit; it is of such a nature.

When the Buddha preached this Dharma, immeasurable multitudes of humans and devas attained the purity of the Dharma-eye, the stage of nature, and the stage of faith; hundreds of thousands of people all attained Great Emptiness and the Great Practice of a Bodhisattva.

Chapter Three: The Bodhisattva’s Teaching and Transformation. From the *Benevolent Kings’ Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra for the Protection of the State*, Chapter Three, the Bodhisattva’s Teaching and Transformation, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
How does a bodhisattva who protects the practice of the ten stages proceed in what should be practiced?
How does he proceed in transforming sentient beings?
By what characteristics are sentient beings to be transformed?
The Buddha said,
“Great King!
These five patiences are the dharmas of a bodhisattva:”

The upper, middle, and lower grades of the patience of submission (*kṣānti*); the upper, middle, and lower grades of the patience of faith (*śraddhā-kṣānti*); the upper, middle, and lower grades of the patience of conformity (*anuloma-kṣānti*); the upper, middle, and lower grades of the patience of non-arising (*anutpāda-kṣānti*); and the upper and lower grades of the patience of quiescent extinction (*nirvāṇa-kṣānti*)—these are called the practice of the *prajñāpāramitā* by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.

“Good son! When they first give rise to the thought of faith, sentient beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges cultivate and subdue themselves through the patience of submission (*kṣānti*). Within the Three Jewels, they develop the ten minds of the nature of the seeds of cultivation:

the mind of faith, the mind of diligence, the mind of mindfulness, the mind of wisdom, the mind of concentration, the mind of giving, the mind of precepts, the mind of protection, the mind of aspiration, and the mind of dedication.”
This is how a bodhisattva, though able to transform only a small number of sentient beings, has already surpassed all the wholesome stages of the two vehicles.
All Buddhas and bodhisattvas nurture ten minds as the holy embryo.

"In the gradual arising of the nature of the lineage of dry wisdom (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā-gotra*), there are ten mental states: namely, the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*)—of body, sensation, mind, and phenomena; the [contemplations of] impurity, suffering, impermanence, and non-self;
the three foundations of mindfulness;
and the three roots of goodness: loving-kindness, generosity, and wisdom."

The three foundations of mindfulness refer to the three periods of time: the patience regarding causes in the past, the patience regarding causes and effects in the present, and the patience regarding effects in the future.

Such a bodhisattva is also able to transform all sentient beings; having already transcended the conceptualizations of self, person, knower, and sentient beings, they cannot be undermined by the inverted views of external paths.

Furthermore, there are ten kinds of the ground of the nature of the path, namely: observing form, consciousness, perception, sensation, and mental formations, one attains the patience of precepts, the patience of knowledge and vision, the patience of concentration, the patience of wisdom, and the patience of liberation;
observing the causes and effects of the three realms, one attains the patience of emptiness, the patience of wishlessness, and the patience of signlessness;
and observing the reality and unreality of the two truths—that all phenomena are impermanent—is called the patience of impermanence.
All phenomena are empty, and they attain the patience of non-arising.
These Bodhisattvas, through their ten firm minds, become wheel-turning kings; they are also able to transform the four continents and give rise to the roots of goodness in all sentient beings.

Furthermore, the Bodhisattva of Faith and Patience—known as one who is skillful, proficient, enlightened, and a practitioner of the Middle Way—severs the bonds of the afflictions of form within the three realms. He is able to manifest in hundreds, thousands, or tens of thousands of Buddha-lands, appearing in hundreds, thousands, or tens of thousands of bodies, possessing immeasurable supernatural powers and merit. He always takes the fifteen mental states as his primary focus:
the four methods of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), the four immeasurable minds (*apramāṇa-citta*), the four great vows (*mahāpraṇidhāna*), and the three gates of liberation (*vimokṣamukha*).
From the stage of the wholesome ground up to omniscience (*sarvajñā*), these fifteen minds serve as the fundamental seeds for all practices.

Furthermore, the Bodhisattva of "Conformity Patience" (*anulomikī-kṣānti*) is said to perceive the superior Dharma of the present life; because he is able to sever the bonds of afflictions such as the mind within the triple world, he manifests a single body throughout the Buddha-fields of the ten directions, employing immeasurable and ineffable supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) to transform sentient beings.

Furthermore, for a Bodhisattva who has attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), there is what is called the far-reaching, immovable contemplative wisdom; because they have also severed the habitual tendencies of afflictions regarding mind and form within the three realms, they manifest unspeakably unspeakable meritorious virtues and supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
"Furthermore, regarding the patience of quiescence (*śānti-kṣānti*): both Buddhas and Bodhisattvas employ this patience to enter the Vajra-samādhi.

Practicing within the lower patience is termed being a Bodhisattva; practicing within the upper patience is termed being Sarvajña (Omniscience). Together they contemplate the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), severing the mental habit-energies (*vāsanā*) of the three realms. The characteristic of the exhaustion of ignorance is the Vajra; the characteristic of the exhaustion of characteristics is Sarvajña. Transcending both worldly truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) and ultimate truth, it constitutes the Sarvajña of the eleventh stage."

Awakening is neither existent nor non-existent; it is profoundly serene and pure, eternally abiding and unchanging. It is identical to the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) and equal to the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*). With unconditional great compassion, it teaches and transforms all sentient beings, riding the vehicle of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-yāna*) to come and transform the three realms.

“Good son! The afflictions of all sentient beings do not transcend the treasury of the triple world; the twenty-two faculties of the retribution of all sentient beings do not transcend the triple world; and the Dharma-body of the response and transformation bodies of all Buddhas likewise does not transcend the triple world.”
If there were no sentient beings outside the three realms, what would the Buddha have to transform?

Therefore, I say that there is a separate treasury of the realm of sentient beings outside the three realms; this is taught in the *Mahāvaipulya* sutras of the non-Buddhists, and was not spoken by the seven Buddhas.
"Great King!
I have always said:
those among all sentient beings who have severed the afflictions of the three realms and exhausted their karmic retributions are called Buddhas;
The intrinsic purity is named the awakening to the nature of *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge).

The fundamental karma of sentient beings is the fundamental karma of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas; it is that which was originally practiced, wherein the fourteen patiences (*kṣānti*) among the five patiences are fully perfected.
He addressed the Buddha, saying,
“How does a bodhisattva purify their fundamental karma to transform sentient beings?
The Buddha said:

"From the first stage up to the final stage, because one possesses all-knowing vision regarding both one's own sphere of practice and the sphere of practice of the Buddhas. Regarding 'original karma':

if a bodhisattva dwells in the lands of a hundred Buddhas, acts as a Caturmahārājika king of Jambudvīpa, cultivates a hundred dharma-gates, and transforms all sentient beings with a mind of equality toward the two truths;

if a bodhisattva dwells in the lands of a thousand Buddhas, acts as a Trāyastriṃśa king, cultivates a thousand dharma-gates, and transforms all sentient beings through the ten paths of wholesome action."

If a bodhisattva dwells in a hundred thousand buddha-fields, he becomes the king of the Suyāma Heaven, cultivates a hundred thousand dharma-gates, and transforms all sentient beings through the four dhyānas;

if a bodhisattva dwells in ten billion buddha-fields, he becomes the king of the Tuṣita Heaven, cultivates ten billion dharma-gates, and transforms all sentient beings by practicing the factors of the path;

if a bodhisattva dwells in a thousand billion buddha-fields, he becomes the king of the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, cultivates a thousand billion dharma-gates, and transforms all sentient beings through the two truths, the four truths, and the eight truths.

If a bodhisattva dwells in a hundred trillion buddha-fields, acting as the king of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin heaven, they cultivate a hundred trillion dharma-gates, using the wisdom of the twelve links of dependent origination to transform all sentient beings;

if a bodhisattva dwells in a million billion buddha-fields, acting as the king of the first dhyāna, they cultivate a million billion dharma-gates, using the wisdom of skillful means and the wisdom of vows to transform all sentient beings;

if a bodhisattva dwells in as many buddha-fields as there are motes of dust in a million worlds, acting as the Brahmā king of the second dhyāna, they cultivate as many dharma-gates as there are motes of dust in a million worlds, using the wisdom of simultaneous illumination through skillful means and supernormal powers to transform all sentient beings.

If a Bodhisattva dwells in as many Buddha-lands as there are atoms in ten million billion *asaṃkhyeya* worlds, acting as a Great Brahmā King of the Third Dhyāna, cultivating as many Dharma-gates as there are atoms in ten million billion *asaṃkhyeya* worlds, and transforming all sentient beings through the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge;

or if a Bodhisattva dwells in as many Buddha-lands as are unspeakably unspeakable, acting as the Great Śāntideva King of the Fourth Dhyāna and Lord of the Three Realms, cultivating unspeakably unspeakable Dharma-gates, attaining the Samādhi of Exhausted Principle, sharing the sphere of action of the Buddhas, exhausting the source of the Three Realms, and teaching and transforming all sentient beings according to the realm of a Buddha.

Therefore, the fundamental practice of transformation of all Bodhisattvas is pure; if the Tathāgatas of the ten directions also cultivate this practice, they will attain the fruit of sarvajñā, become kings of the three realms, and transform all immeasurable sentient beings.

At that time, a great assembly as numerous as the sands of ten million billion Ganges Rivers rose from their seats, scattering immeasurable and inconceivable flowers and burning immeasurable and inconceivable incense as offerings to Śākyamuni Buddha and the immeasurable great bodhisattvas. With palms joined, they listened to King Prasenajit’s exposition of the Prajñāpāramitā, and now, before the Buddha, they praised him in verse:
“The World-Honored One, the Guide, whose body is adamantine, Whose mental activity is quiescent, turns the wheel of Dharma;
With the eightfold eloquence and a majestic voice, he speaks for the sake of the multitude, And at this moment, hundreds of billions attain the Way.”
At that time, six celestial beings left the household life for the Way, becoming a community of bhikṣus practicing the bodhisattva path.
Regarding the wondrous Dharma-gate of the merits of the five patiences, fourteen noble beings were able to comprehend it clearly;
they practiced within the patience of the three stages of worthiness and the ten stages of sagehood, yet only the Buddha alone can exhaustively fathom its source.
The Buddha, the Sangha, and the Dharma—the ocean of teachings and the treasury of the Triple Gem—contain within them immeasurable merit.
When Bodhisattvas of the ten wholesome paths resolve their great mind, they forever part from the ocean of the suffering wheel of the triple world.
Those with middling or lower grades of the ten wholesome acts become minor kings; those with the superior grade of the ten wholesome acts become Iron-Wheel Kings.
The copper-wheel king of the lineage of practice rules over two worlds; the silver-wheel king of the nature-lineage rules over three;
the wheel-turning king of the lineage of the path, firm in virtue, possesses the seven treasures and golden light, ruling over the four worlds.
The thirty stages of the noble embryo of the submissive patience (*kṣānti*) consist of the ten faiths, the ten cessations, and the ten firm minds;
all Buddhas of the three periods of time traverse within them, for there is none who does not arise from this submissive patience.
The source and origin of all bodhisattva practices—therefore, it is difficult to give rise to the mind of faith.
If one attains this faith, one will certainly not regress;
entering the first stage of the path of non-arising, one teaches and transforms sentient beings while walking in awakening. This is called the bodhisattva’s initial resolve.
The Bodhisattva Good Awakening, a Heavenly King of the Four Quarters, Shines simultaneously upon the equal path of the two truths;
Through skillful means he transforms sentient beings as he travels through a hundred lands, And has now first ascended the signless path of the One Vehicle.
The wisdom that enters into principle is called "abiding"; abiding gives rise to virtuous conduct, which is called "ground.
Abiding in the first [ground] with a single mind fulfills virtuous conduct, remaining unmoved within the ultimate truth.
The Bodhisattva Li-da, King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, manifests forms throughout the six realms and a thousand lands;
he is the third truth—without conditions and without marks—wherein there is no non-existence, no birth, and no dualistic illumination.
The Heavenly King Yantian, whose bright wisdom illuminates emptiness, manifests forms throughout the myriad lands to guide all living beings.
With a mind of forbearance free from duality within the Three Truths, he emerges from existence and enters non-existence through transformative birth.
The three types of practitioners—the Well-Awakened, the Detached, and the Luminous—are able to extinguish the afflictions of form within the triple world;
yet they further contemplate the forms of body and speech within the triple world, for the nature of phenomena is supreme and leaves nothing unilluminated.
Blazing Wisdom, Sublime Light, and Great Diligence; The King of Tuṣita travels through billions of lands.
With true wisdom, he contemplates the quiescence of conditions and the path of skillful means; He realizes non-arising and illuminates emptiness while understanding existence.
With supreme wisdom, he personally realizes and clarifies the three truths;

as king of the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations over ten billion lands, he contemplates the truth of emptiness within emptiness as being without dual characteristics, manifesting transformations throughout the six realms of existence while entering the Avīci Hell.
The Bodhisattva Dharmākara, Sovereign King, Non-dual and non-illuminating, he penetrates the emptiness of principle;
The great light of wisdom, with the three truths manifest before him, Illumines billions of lands and teaches all beings.
The Samādhi of the Manifestation of the Supreme Dharma of Flames Can wash away the delusions and afflictions of the deluded minds within the three realms;
With the wisdom of emptiness, one dwells in tranquil non-conditioned contemplation, And returns to contemplate the emptiness of the mind and its immeasurable retribution.
Reaching far to the Unborn, the King of the First Dhyāna, He constantly teaches sentient beings across ten trillion lands.
With his reward body yet to be fully delivered, one lifetime remains; He enters the stage of the Flow of Dharma through Equal Contemplation.
Having first entered the objectless Vajra-patience, one shall never again receive a retributive body within the three realms;
observing the third meaning with non-dual illumination, one practices the twenty-one births of emptiness and quiescence.
The concentration that accords with the Path through the habituation of craving for the three realms is far-reaching; the True Person alone realizes it clearly.
The Bodhisattva King of the Second Dhyāna contemplates with equanimity, transforming his birth-body into a Dharma-body of immeasurable light.
Entering a hundred Ganges-sands of lands to transform all beings, Perfectly illuminating the events of all three periods throughout eternal kalpas,
Reflecting back upon the joyful, inexhaustible source of emptiness, One remains eternally tranquil within the third truth.
The Bodhisattva Wisdom-Light, King of the Third Dhyāna, Can manifest a thousand Ganges-sands of worlds at once;
Ever abiding in the practice of unconditioned emptiness and stillness, He comprehends the Buddha-treasuries of the Ganges-sands in a single thought-moment.
The Bodhisattva King of the Four Dhyānas, having received empowerment, transforms sentient beings across billions of Ganges-sands of lands;
having first entered the Vajra stage where all is fully realized, he has forever transcended twenty-nine births.
Within the patience of tranquil extinction, one contemplates with the lower patience; A single turn brings the wondrous enlightenment, eternally serene.
The three grades of practitioners receive the empowerment of equal wisdom, Eliminating the remaining habitual tendencies and the conditions of ignorance.
Because ignorance is the characteristic of habitual tendencies, it is affliction; when the principle of the two truths is fully exhausted, everything ceases.
Perfect wisdom is signless, the King of the Three Realms; with thirty births ended, one attains Great Enlightenment.
The Great Quiescence, the Unconditioned Vajragarbha, Whose infinite compassion exhausts all karmic retribution;
In the ultimate truth he is ever peaceful and secure, And within him abides wondrous wisdom that exhausts the source and fulfills the nature.
The three sages and ten saints dwell in the retribution of their fruits; Only the Buddha alone dwells in the Pure Land.
All sentient beings dwell temporarily in the retribution realm; Upon ascending to the Vajra Ground, they dwell in the Pure Land.
The Tathāgata’s virtues of the three karmas are infinite;
I, Candraprabha, now pay homage to the Triple Gem—the Unsurpassed Dharma King, the tree among men, who covers the great assembly with immeasurable light.
His mouth constantly preaches the Dharma, never without meaning; his mind and wisdom are quiescent, illuminating without conditions.
The Lion among Men speaks for the sake of the multitude, and the great assembly, filled with joy, scatters golden flowers.
A hundred billion lands shook in six ways, and all living beings received wondrous rewards;
the World-Honored One joyfully spoke of the fourteen kings, and for this reason I now briefly praise the Buddha.

At that time, the great assembly, having heard King Candraprabha extol the immeasurable treasury of merits of the fourteen kings, attained the great benefit of the Dharma. Thereupon, within that very assembly, ten *gaṅgā*-sands of celestial kings, ten *gaṅgā*-sands of Brahmā kings, and ten *gaṅgā*-sands of ghost-king spirits, as well as those from the three lower realms, attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

Among the eight classes of beings, the Asura kings manifested their ghostly forms to receive the Way in the heavens; some entered the stage of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*) after three births, others after four, five, or even ten births, attaining the nature of a noble one (*ārya*) and realizing all immeasurable rewards.
The Buddha addressed the assembly of devas who had attained the fruits of the Path: "Good sons!

In the past, throughout ten thousand kalpas, during the Dharma of King Dragon-Radiance (Nāgaprabhāsa), this King Moonlight (Candraprabha) was a bodhisattva of the fourth stage, while I was a bodhisattva of the eighth stage."
"Now, before me, you have let out a great lion's roar. It is so, it is so!
Just as you have said, you have attained the discourse on the true meaning; it is inconceivable and immeasurable, known only by Buddhas and Buddhas."

“Good son! That which is taught—the fourteen *prajñāpāramitās*, the thirty *kṣāntis* of the three grades (upper, middle, and lower) of the stages of the three *kṣāntis*, the treasury of all practices, and the treasury of all Buddhas—is inconceivable.”

Why is this? Because all Buddhas are born therein, cease therein, and manifest transformations therein; yet they are without birth, without cessation, and without transformation. They have no self and no other; they are supreme and non-dual. They are neither transformed nor untransformed, neither with marks nor without marks, and they neither come nor go, for they are like empty space.

All sentient beings are without birth and without cessation, without bondage and without liberation; they are neither cause nor effect, yet not without cause and effect. This is because afflictions, the self, the person, knowledge and views, the experiencer, and that which belongs to the self are all empty in their practice of suffering.

The collection of all phenomena is the illusory transformation of the five aggregates; they neither aggregate nor disperse, for phenomena are identical to the dharma-nature, being quiescent and empty.

The realm of phenomena is empty—empty and signless; it does not revolve, it is not inverted, and it does not conform to illusory transformations. It is like space: there is no Triple Gem, no sages, and no six realms of existence.

Prajñā has no cognition and no vision; it does not function and does not take objects as conditions; it is not based on causes and is not received, because it does not attain any characteristic of appearance. Thus, practicing the Way is practicing the characteristic of the Way which is like empty space.
Since the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) are thus, how could there be practice with a mind or practice without a mind?

Therefore, the merit of *prajñā* cannot be practiced by acting within the realm of sentient beings; it cannot be practiced by acting within the phenomena of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*); it cannot be practiced by acting within objective conditions (*viṣaya*); and it cannot be practiced by acting within understanding.
Therefore, Prajñā is inconceivable; and because all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas practice within it, they too are inconceivable.
That all Tathāgatas manifest within the illusory and non-abiding dharmas is likewise inconceivable.

“Good son! As for this treasury of merit, even if bodhisattvas of the thirteenth stage of consecration, as numerous as the sands of immeasurable Ganges Rivers, were to speak of these merits, it would be like a single drop in the ocean compared to the hundred thousand billionth part of what you, O King, have spoken.”
I now briefly describe the merit of these sections of meaning; it brings great benefit to all sentient beings and is likewise approved by the immeasurable Tathāgatas of the past, future, and present.
The immeasurable praise of the three worthies and ten sages is the merit pertaining to the portion of King Candraprabha. "Good son!

These fourteen dharma-gates have been cultivated and accumulated by all sentient beings, all followers of the three vehicles, and all Buddhas of the three periods of time; it shall be the same for all future Buddhas."
If all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas were not to attain *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge) by means of this gate, it would be impossible. Why?
Because there is no other path for any Buddha or Bodhisattva.

Therefore, all good sons, if there are those who hear these various gates of patience—the patience of faith, the patience of cessation, the patience of firmness, the patience of excellent awakening, the patience of detached penetration, the patience of clear wisdom, the patience of blazing wisdom, the patience of supreme wisdom, the patience of the manifestation of dharmas, the patience of far-reaching penetration, the patience of equal awakening, the patience of the light of wisdom, the patience of consecration, and the patience of perfect awakening—such persons shall transcend the suffering and hardship of hundreds, thousands, and immeasurable Ganges-sands of lifetimes over ten million kalpas; having entered this Dharma-gate, they shall obtain the retribution in their present body.

At that time, among the assembly were ten billion bodhisattvas, all named Gaganagañjagarbhasāgara. Rejoicing in the joy of the Dharma, they each scattered flowers into the air, which transformed into immeasurable flower pedestals. Upon these stood immeasurable multitudes who expounded the fourteen right practices.

The eighteen Brahmās and the kings of the six heavens of desire also scattered precious flowers; each sat upon a terrace in mid-air, expounding the fourteen right practices, receiving, upholding, reading, and reciting them, and understanding their underlying principles.
Innumerable spirits and deities manifest their bodies to practice the *prajñāpāramitā*.
The Buddha said to the Great King:
"You previously stated:..."
"What is meant by 'transforming sentient beings through their characteristics'?
If one perceives a phantom-like body as a phantom-like being, this is the Bodhisattva’s true practice of transforming sentient beings.

At the very first moment of a sentient being's consciousness, that consciousness differs from wood or stone; it gives rise to innate goodness and innate evil. Evil serves as the root of immeasurable unwholesome consciousnesses, while goodness serves as the root of immeasurable wholesome consciousnesses.

From the first moment of the vajra until the final moment, therein arise unspeakably unspeakable numbers of consciousnesses, which form the matter and mind of sentient beings; this is the root of sentient beings.
Form is called the veil of form; mind is called the veil of consciousness, the veil of perception, the veil of feeling, and the veil of formations.
A "veil" functions by way of obscuring and covering; "body" (kāya) is named for its nature as a collection.
“Great King! This single dharma of form gives rise to immeasurable forms:

that which is apprehended by the eye is form; that which is apprehended by the ear is sound; that which is apprehended by the nose is fragrance; that which is apprehended by the tongue is flavor; that which is apprehended by the body is tangibility; that which is firm and stable is called earth; that which is moist is called water; that which is hot is called fire; and that which is light and mobile is called wind.”
That which gives rise to the five consciousnesses is called a faculty (*indriya*).
In this way, within a single form and a single mind, there are inconceivable forms and minds.
"Great King!..."
Because the six consciousnesses of ordinary beings are coarse, they perceive immeasurable conventional material phenomena such as blue, yellow, square, and round, which are merely provisional names;
because the six consciousnesses of noble ones are pure, they perceive real phenomena, including all actual material phenomena such as form, fragrance, taste, and touch.
"Sentient beings" is a designation of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
Whether they exist or do not exist, it is merely the arising of the notion of "sentient beings" that is called conventional truth.

Because conventional truth is provisional, deceptive, and illusory, it exists; even the six realms of existence are illusory transformations. Sentient beings see these illusory transformations, and illusory transformations see illusory transformations. The Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, spirits, the self, and form-and-mind—these are called the truth of illusion (*māyā-satya*); as for the phenomena of the truth of illusion, they have no inherent existence.
Before the Buddha appeared in the world, there were no names and no names with meaning;

all phenomena were illusory transformations, lacking names, lacking essence or characteristics, lacking the names of the three realms, and lacking the names of the six destinies as the retribution for good and evil.
“Great King!
For this reason, as each Buddha appears in the world for the sake of sentient beings, they speak of the names of the three realms and the six paths of existence.
These are called immeasurable names, such as the dharmas of space, the four great elements, mind-dharmas, and form-dharmas.”

The dharmas of continuous succession are neither identical nor different; for if they were identical, there would be no succession, and if they were different, there would likewise be no succession. Because they are neither identical nor different, they are called the truth of continuous succession.

Relative conventional dharmas are all termed "relative," and they are also termed "indeterminate relative," such as the dharmas of the five colors and so forth, including all dharmas such as existence and non-existence.

All phenomena are dependently originated; sentient beings are conventionally established through both simultaneous and sequential causes and conditions, as well as the virtues and evils of the three periods of time—all of which are illusory transformations. These are the sentient beings of the truth of illusion.
“Great King!

If a bodhisattva perceives sentient beings as illusory transformations as described above—all of which are false and deceptive, like flowers in the sky—then even the five eyes of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the ten stages see them as such through the truth of illusion; such is the manner in which a bodhisattva transforms sentient beings.”

When this Dharma was being taught, immeasurable devaputras and the great assembly attained the patience of acquiescence (*kṣānti*), attained the patience of emptiness and non-arising (*śūnyatā-anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), and [realized] the ineffable virtues and practices of the first through the tenth stages (*bhūmi*).
Chapter Four: The Two Truths, from the *Benevolent Kings’ Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra for the Protection of the State*. At that time, King Prasenajit said:
"Is there conventional truth within ultimate truth?"
If one says it does not exist, then wisdom should not be dual;
if one says it exists, then wisdom should not be singular.
As for the meaning of "one" and "two," what is their reality?
The Buddha told the Great King:
"Regarding the one meaning and two meanings you previously asked of the seven Buddhas of the past,
you do not listen now, and I shall not speak now."
There is neither hearing nor speaking, for this constitutes both a single meaning and a dual meaning.
Listen attentively, listen attentively!
Contemplate it well and practice in accordance with the Dharma.
The verses of the Seven Buddhas are as follows:
"The ultimate truth is signless; It is neither self-made nor made by another.
Dependent origination is inherently present; It is neither self-made nor made by another."
The nature of phenomena is fundamentally without nature; it is like the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*).
All that exists is originally a phenomenon; through the collection of the three provisionalities, there is provisional existence.
There is no non-existence, for the truth is truly non-existent; it is quiescent extinction, the supreme emptiness.
All phenomena exist through causes and conditions; such is the meaning of existence and non-existence.
Existence and non-existence are fundamentally two, like the two horns of an ox;
yet when illuminated by understanding, they are seen as non-dual, for the two truths are never identical.
Understanding the mind, one sees non-duality; seeking duality, it cannot be found.
It is not that the two truths are one, nor can there be a "not-two" to be attained.
In understanding, there is always only oneness; in the truths, there is always only duality.
To penetrate this non-duality is to truly enter the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
Conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) arises like a magical illusion;
it is like flowers in the sky, or like a shadow, or like a third hand—non-existent, yet appearing as if existent through the deception of causes and conditions.
Seeing an illusion as an illusion, sentient beings call it the "illusory truth.
When a magician sees the illusory phenomena, they find no reality in them at all;
this is called the contemplation of the Buddhas, and the contemplation of Bodhisattvas is likewise.
"Great King!
Within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva constantly illuminates the two truths (*dvaya-satya*) to transform sentient beings.
The Buddha and sentient beings are one and not two."
Why is this? Because sentient beings are empty, one can establish the emptiness of bodhi; because bodhi is empty, one can establish the emptiness of sentient beings.
Because all dharmas are empty, there is the emptiness of emptiness.

Why is this? Because *prajñā* is signless and the two truths are empty; *prajñā* is empty because from ignorance (*avidyā*) up to omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), there is neither self-characteristic nor other-characteristic. When the five eyes are perfected, one sees that there is nothing to be seen. One does not accept practice, nor does one accept non-practice, nor does one accept neither practice nor non-practice, and so on, up to not accepting any phenomena whatsoever.
When a bodhisattva has not yet attained buddhahood, they take awakening (bodhi) to be affliction; when a bodhisattva has attained buddhahood, they take affliction to be awakening.
Why is this? Because in the ultimate sense (paramārtha), there is non-duality, for all Buddhas, Tathāgatas, and indeed all phenomena, are suchness (tathatā).
He addressed the Buddha, saying:
“How is it that the Tathāgatas of the ten directions and all bodhisattvas practice the characteristics of all dharmas without departing from words? “Great King!
The Wheel of Dharma consists of:

the suchness of the *dharmapada*, the suchness of the *geya*, the suchness of the *vyākaraṇa*, the suchness of the *gāthā* not recited [as prose], the suchness of the *udāna* spoken spontaneously without being asked, the suchness of the *śīlaskandha*, the suchness of the *avadāna*, the suchness of the *itivṛttaka*, the suchness of the *jātaka*, the suchness of the *vaipulya*, the suchness of the *adbhutadharma*, and the suchness of the *upadeśa*. These are called the suchness of all names, phrases, syllables, sounds, fruits, letters, and recorded sentences.
If one grasps at words and letters, one does not practice emptiness.
"Great King!
Just as the words and letters cultivate the Mother of the Buddhas' Wisdom, so too the fundamental wisdom of the nature of all sentient beings is the very essence of *sarvajñā* (omniscience)."

Before the Buddhas have attained Buddhahood, they take the future Buddha as the mother of wisdom; that which is not yet attained is their nature (*dharmatā*), and that which has already been attained is omniscience (*sarvajñā*).
The *prajñā* of the three vehicles is neither born nor extinguished; its self-nature is eternally abiding.
Because all sentient beings take this as their awakened nature (*bodhicitta*).

If a bodhisattva is without reception and without words, transcending words yet not being non-words, and practices non-practice as the practice of words, they attain the true nature of Prajñā, the Prajñāpāramitā.
"Great King!
If a bodhisattva protects the Buddha, protects the transformation of sentient beings, and protects the practices of the ten stages, it is as such.
He addressed the Buddha, saying:
“There are immeasurable classes of sentient beings; their faculties are immeasurable, and their practices are also immeasurable.
Is this Dharma-gate one, two, or immeasurable?
“Great King! [The Buddha replied:]
The gateways for contemplating all phenomena are neither one nor two, but are indeed immeasurable.
All phenomena are neither characterized by marks nor are they not without marks.
If a Bodhisattva perceives sentient beings as being either one or two, they fail to see that which is neither one nor two—this absence of both one and two is the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*).
“Great King!
Whether ‘existence’ or ‘non-existence,’ these belong to the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).

Because all phenomena are subsumed within three truths—the truth of emptiness (*śūnya-tattva*), the truth of form (*rūpa-tattva*), and the truth of mind (*citta-tattva*)—I say that all phenomena do not transcend these three truths.”

I and others know and see that the five aggregates of clinging are empty, up to and including the emptiness of all dharmas; because the faculties and practices of various classes of sentient beings differ, there are dharma-gates that are neither one nor two.
“Great King!
The seven Buddhas taught the Mahāprajñāpāramitā, and I now teach the Prajñāpāramitā; there is no duality and no distinction between them.
You and this great assembly should receive, uphold, recite, and explain it.”

Regarding the merit of this sutra: there are immeasurable, unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddhas; each and every Buddha teaches and transforms immeasurable, unspeakably unspeakable numbers of sentient beings, and each and every one of those sentient beings attains Buddhahood.
Those Buddhas, in turn, teach and transform immeasurable, unspeakably unspeakable numbers of sentient beings, and they all attain Buddhahood.
These aforementioned three types of Buddhas have preached eighty trillion verses of the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra.
Within a single verse, one may further divide it into a thousand parts;
even within a single part, the meaning of its phrases cannot be fully exhausted—how much more so for one who gives rise to a single thought of faith in this sutra!

These sentient beings surpass the merits of a hundred, a thousand, or ten *kalpas* and the stages of the ten grounds; how much more so the merits of those who receive, uphold, read, recite, explain, and expound it—these are equal to the Buddhas of the ten directions and no different from them.
"You should know that such a person is indeed a Tathāgata; they shall attain Buddhahood before long.
At that time, when the great assembly heard this sutra being preached, ten billion people attained the patience of the three emptinesses (*trīṇi śūnyatā-kṣāntayaḥ*);
one hundred trillion people attained the patience of great emptiness (*mahāśūnyatā-kṣānti*) and the nature of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).
“Great King!
This sutra is titled ‘The Sutra on the Perfection of Wisdom Requested by the Benevolent Kings.

You all should receive and uphold this Perfection of Wisdom Sutra; this sutra possesses immeasurable merit. It is called the merit of protecting the state, and it is also called the merit of serving as the medicinal remedy for all kings, which, when applied, provides great protection for dwellings and also protects the bodies of all sentient beings.”
This very Prajñāpāramitā is the protection of the land, like a city’s moats, walls, swords, spears, and shields; you should uphold the Prajñāpāramitā in this same manner.
