Chapter Five: On Protecting the State.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Great King:
"Listen well; I shall now correctly explain the methods for protecting the state. You should receive and uphold the Prajñāpāramitā."

When the land is about to fall into chaos, when it is destroyed by the fires of the kalpa, or when bandits come to ravage the kingdom, one should invite a hundred images of the Buddha, a hundred images of bodhisattvas, a hundred images of arhats, and a hundred assemblies of bhikṣus; let the fourfold assembly and the seven classes of disciples listen together, and invite a hundred Dharma masters to lecture on the Prajñāpāramitā.

Before the high seat, he lit a hundred lamps, burned a hundred blended incenses, and offered a hundred varieties of colored flowers as an offering to the Triple Gem; he provided the three robes and daily requisites for the Dharma Master, and likewise served light meals and midday meals at the proper times.
"Great King!

If you recite and study this sutra twice each day, there are one hundred classes of spirits within your kingdom, and each of these classes consists of another hundred members who delight in hearing this sutra; these spirits will protect your kingdom."
“Great King!

When a kingdom is in turmoil, first the spirits and deities fall into disorder; because the spirits and deities are in disorder, the myriad people fall into disorder; bandits come to plunder the country, and the common folk perish and are lost.”

Ministers, rulers, crown princes, sons of kings, and the hundred officials collectively give rise to what is right and wrong; heaven and earth manifest strange anomalies; the twenty-eight lunar mansions, the celestial paths, the sun, and the moon lose their proper seasons and measurements; and many rebellions and bandits arise.
“Great King!
In the event of dangers from fire, water, wind, or any other such calamities, you should likewise recite and study this sutra; the ritual application is as previously described.
Great King!”

Not only does it protect the nation, but it also protects one's merit. Whether seeking wealth, nobility, official rank, or the fulfillment of the seven treasures; seeking sons or daughters; seeking wisdom, understanding, and renown; or seeking the retributive fruits of the six heavens and the nine grades of bliss among humans—one should likewise recite this sutra, with the ritual application as previously described.
"Great King!

It not only protects merit, but also guards against various calamities. Whether it be the suffering of illness, being bound by cangues, fetters, or shackles; having committed the four grave offenses, created the causes for the five heinous crimes, or incurred the sins of the eight difficulties; or engaging in the affairs of the six realms—all such immeasurable sufferings and calamities can be averted by reciting this sutra, with the ritual application as previously described."
"Great King!
In the past, there was a king named Śakra Devānām Indra, who, for the sake of King Mūrdhaja, ascended to heaven intending to destroy his kingdom.

At that time, the Heavenly King Śakra, employing the methods used by the Buddhas of the seven generations, arranged one hundred high seats and invited one hundred Dharma masters to lecture on the Prajñāpāramitā."
Mūrdhaja immediately fell from his position, as described in the *Pāpadeśanā-sūtra*: "Great King!
In the past, there was a king named Tārā who had a crown prince wishing to ascend the throne, the first of whom was named Pāṇḍu."
The Crown Prince was instructed by his teacher, the non-Buddhist Rādha, that he must take the heads of a thousand kings to sacrifice to the household deity.
Since ascending the throne, he had already obtained the heads of nine hundred and ninety-nine kings, lacking only one.
He traveled north for ten thousand *li* and encountered a king named King Universal Radiance (*Samantaprabha*).
King Universal Radiance said to King Spotless Feet (*Vimalapāda*):
"I pray that you will permit me for one day to provide food for the śramaṇas and pay homage to the Triple Gem."
King Banzu granted him one day.

At that time, King Puming, following the Dharma of the seven past Buddhas, invited a hundred Dharma masters and prepared a hundred high seats; for two periods each day, they lectured on the *Prajñāpāramitā*: “When the kalpa-ending conflagration has run its course, Heaven and earth burn through and through.”
Mount Sumeru and the vast oceans shall all be reduced to ashes; when the merit of devas and nāgas is exhausted, they perish therein.
If even the two polarities of heaven and earth fall, how can there be any permanence in a kingdom?
Birth, old age, sickness, and death revolve without end; Matters conflict with one's wishes, and sorrow and grief cause harm.
Desire is deep and calamity is heavy; like sores and ulcers, there is nothing external to them. The three realms are all suffering;
what reliance can there be in this kingdom?
That which exists has its origin in non-existence; all things are formed through causes and conditions. That which flourishes must inevitably decline; that which is full must inevitably become empty.
Sentient beings, in their bustling confusion, are all like dwellings in an illusion. Sounds and echoes are both void; so too are the lands.
The consciousness-spirit has no form; it temporarily rides upon the four serpents, taking the precious elephant of ignorance as its pleasure-carriage.
The body has no permanent master, and the spirit has no permanent home. Since body and spirit are already separated, how could there be a nation?

At that time, when the Dharma Master had finished reciting these verses, the retinue of King Samantaprabha attained the emptiness of the Dharma-eye; the king himself realized the meditative concentration equal to space, and through hearing the Dharma, he attained awakening and understanding.
Returning to the assembly before King Bimbisāra in the kingdom of Tāmraliptī, he immediately addressed the nine hundred and ninety-nine kings, saying:
"The time for our departure has arrived; each of you should recite the verses from the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra on the Benevolent Kings' Questions* as spoken by the seven past Buddhas."
Then King Pañcāṅga asked the various kings,
"What teachings do you all recite?
At that time, King Samantaprabha answered the king with the aforementioned verse.
Upon hearing this Dharma, King [Bimbisāra] attained the samādhi of emptiness;
the nine hundred and ninety-nine other kings, having likewise heard the Dharma, all realized the concentration of the three gates of emptiness.
At that time, King Pañcāla was filled with immense joy and addressed the other kings, saying:
"I have been misled by non-Buddhist teachers of heterodox views; it is not your fault.
You may return to your respective countries and each invite a Dharma Master to lecture on the names, meanings, and phrases of the Prajñāpāramitā."

At that time, King Pañcaśikha entrusted the kingdom to his younger brother, left the household life to practice the Way, and realized the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), as described in the section on the Ten Kings.
Five thousand kings constantly recited this sutra and received its retribution in their present lives.
"Great King!
The sixteen great kings cultivate the Dharma for protecting the state; such is the proper way of the Dharma, which you should uphold.
All sentient beings within the six realms of existence—both among devas and humans—should likewise receive and uphold the names, phrases, and syllables of the seven Buddhas."
In future ages, there will be immeasurable minor kings who wish to protect their kingdoms; those who are likewise situated should invite a Dharma Master to preach the Prajñāpāramitā.

At that time, when Śākyamuni Buddha was preaching the Prajñāpāramitā, five billion people among the assembly attained entry into the first bhūmi. Furthermore, eight hundred thousand sons of the gods from the six heavens of the desire realm attained the stage of the ground of nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā-bhūmi*). Additionally, eighteen Brahmā kings attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) and the patience of the joy of the dharma of non-arising. Moreover, there were those who had previously studied as bodhisattvas and realized the first, second, third, and even up to the tenth bhūmi. Furthermore, the eight classes of *asura* kings attained thirteen gates of samādhi and three gates of samādhi, and having transformed their ghostly bodies, they entered the correct meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) of the heavens. All those present in this assembly attained self-nature faith (*svabhāva-śraddhā*) and even immeasurable faith in emptiness (*ananta-śūnyatā-śraddhā*).
I shall now briefly describe the merits of the devas and others; they cannot be fully exhausted. **Chapter Six:

The Chapter on Scattering Flowers** *The Benevolent Kings’ Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra for the Protection of the State* At that time, when the sixteen great kings heard the Buddha preach the *Prajñāpāramitā* in one hundred trillion verses, they rejoiced immeasurably. They immediately scattered one hundred trillion stems of flowers, which transformed in mid-air into a single seat. The Buddhas of the ten directions sat together upon this seat and preached the *Prajñāpāramitā*.

An immeasurable multitude sat together upon a single seat; they took golden *ra* flowers and scattered them over Śākyamuni Buddha, which formed ten thousand wheel-shaped flowers that served as a canopy above the assembly.

They further scattered eighty-four thousand *prajñāpāramitā* flowers into the air, which transformed into a white cloud pavilion. Within the pavilion, the Buddha King of Radiance (*Prabhāsarāja*), together with an immeasurable multitude, preached the *prajñāpāramitā*.
The multitude in Taizhong held *vajra-roaring* flowers and scattered them over Śākyamuni Buddha and the great assembly;
they then further scattered *wondrous awakening* flowers into the void, which transformed into a vajra city.
Within the city, the Buddha Siṃhanāda, together with the Buddhas of the ten directions and the great bodhisattvas, discussed the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

At that time, the bodhisattvas within the city took up flowers of radiant light and scattered them over Śākyamuni Buddha, forming a single flower pedestal; within this pedestal were the Buddhas of the ten directions.

The various devas scattered celestial flowers, which formed a purple cloud-canopy in the void above Śākyamuni Buddha, covering the trichiliocosm; amidst this canopy, the devas and humans scattered flowers as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, falling down like clouds.

At that time, the various kings, having scattered flowers as an offering, made this vow: "May the Buddhas of the past, the Buddhas of the present, and the Buddhas of the future always proclaim the Prajñāpāramitā. May all those who uphold it—monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen—have their aspirations fulfilled and may they always practice the Prajñāpāramitā."
The Buddha told the Great King:
"So it is, so it is! It is just as you have said."
"The Prajñāpāramitā should be expounded and received; it is the mother of all Buddhas, the mother of all Bodhisattvas, and the source from which the supernormal powers arise.
At that time, the Buddha manifested five inconceivable miraculous transformations for the king:
a single flower entered into immeasurable flowers, and immeasurable flowers entered into a single flower.
A single buddha-field enters into immeasurable buddha-fields, and immeasurable buddha-fields enter into a single buddha-field;
immeasurable buddha-fields enter into the space of a single pore, and the space of a single pore enters into the spaces of immeasurable pores;
immeasurable Mount Sumerus and immeasurable great oceans enter into a mustard seed.

The body of a single Buddha enters the bodies of immeasurable sentient beings; the bodies of immeasurable sentient beings enter the body of a single Buddha, enter the bodies of the six realms of existence, and enter the bodies of earth, water, fire, and wind. The Buddha-body is inconceivable, the bodies of sentient beings are inconceivable, and the worlds are inconceivable.

When the Buddha manifested his supernormal powers, the devas and humans of the ten directions attained the Flower Samādhi; ten *gaṅgā*-sands of bodhisattvas manifested their bodies as Buddhas; three *gaṅgā*-sands of kings of the eight classes of beings realized the path of bodhisattvahood; and ten thousand women manifested their bodies and attained the supernormal power samādhi.
“Good son! This Prajñāpāramitā possesses benefits for the three periods of time; it was taught in the past, is being taught in the present, and will be taught in the future.”
"Listen attentively, listen attentively!
Contemplate this well and practice it according to the Dharma. Chapter Seven:
On Upholding The *Ratnaketuparivarta Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra for the Protection of the State*, Chapter Seven: On Upholding. At that time, Candraprabha thought in his heart and spoke with his mouth:

"I saw Śākyamuni Buddha manifest immeasurable supernatural powers, and I also saw the Buddha Ratnapūrṇa upon the thousand-petaled lotus pedestal; he is the master of the transformation bodies of all Buddhas."
Furthermore, he saw Buddhas upon worlds of a thousand lotus petals, and within them, each of those Buddhas was individually preaching the Prajñāpāramitā.
He addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Such immeasurable Prajñāpāramitā is ineffable and inexplicable; it cannot be known by consciousness."
"How do these good sons clearly understand and awaken to this sutra, and how do they, in accordance with the Dharma, open the path of the dharma of emptiness for all sentient beings?
The Great Muni replied:

"There are good sons who practice the thirteen gates of contemplation; as great Dharma Kings, from the stage of Patience through Arising (Kṣānti-utpāda) up to the Vajra-Apex (Vajraśekhara), they all serve as Dharma Masters, providing support and establishing [the teaching]."
"You, the great assembly, should make offerings to him as you would to the Buddha; you should present to him a hundred trillion celestial flowers and celestial incenses. Good son!"

That Dharma Master is a Bodhisattva of the stage of the lineage of practice (*śikṣāgotra*), whether he be a lay *upāsaka* or *upāsikā*, or an ordained *bhikṣu* or *bhikṣuṇī*. Practicing the ten wholesome paths of action, he observes his own body part by part as impure—earth, water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness.

Furthermore, observing the fourteen faculties—namely, the five sense organs, the five sensations, male, female, mind, and life—he perceives that they possess immeasurable faults and transgressions. Consequently, he gives rise to the unsurpassed bodhicitta; because he constantly cultivates the realization that all things within the three realms are moment by moment impure, he attains the gate of contemplation of the patience regarding impurity (*aśubha-kṣānti-vipaśyanā-mukha*).

Dwelling in the family of the Buddha, they cultivate the six points of harmonious respect—namely, the three karmas being identical in precepts, identical in views, and identical in study—and practice the path of the eighty-four thousand pāramitās.

“Good son! Before attaining the patience of practice (śikṣā-akṣānti), a bodhisattva who practices the ten wholesome paths may regress or advance, just like light feathers that drift east and west with the wind.”

These bodhisattvas are also like this: although they have practiced the ten right paths for ten thousand kalpas and generated the mind of *sambodhi*, they must still enter the stage of *śikṣā-kṣānti* (patience in training) and constantly study the three methods of *kṣānti* (patience); yet they cannot be designated as persons of indeterminate nature.

One who is established in this concentration enters the stage of the emptiness of beings; because they possess the nature of a noble one (*ārya*), they will certainly not commit the five heinous acts, the six grave offenses, or the twenty-eight light offenses.
It is impossible for them to commit the crime of rebellion against the Buddha’s teachings and scriptures, or to claim that these are not the words of the Buddha.
By being able to cultivate the practice of patience on the path of subduing for one asaṃkhyeya kalpa, one first attains entry into the stage of *saṃghāta*.

Furthermore, through the ten wisdom-observations of the nature-seed-lineage (*prakṛti-gotra*), one extinguishes the ten inversions, as well as the various provisional and false conceptions of self, person, and knowledge-and-vision; there is only name, only sensation, and only dharmas, which are unobtainable, lacking fixed characteristics, and devoid of the characteristics of self or other.

He cultivates the contemplation of the protection of emptiness and constantly practices the hundred thousand pāramitās, never departing from them in thought after thought; having practiced the Dharma of the right path for two asaṃkhyeya kalpas, he dwells in the stage of Pāradā.

"Furthermore, while abiding in the firm patience (*kṣānti*) of the lineage of the path-knowledge (*mārgajñatā*), one contemplates that all phenomena are without arising, without abiding, and without cessation. That is to say, the five aggregates of clinging, the three realms, and the two truths lack the characteristics of self or other, because their suchness (*tathatā*) cannot be apprehended;
yet, they constantly enter the tenth [stage], the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), wherein every moment of mind is quiescent, and yet they take birth within the three realms."
Why is this? Because the retribution for the habitual tendencies of karma has not yet been exhausted, they are born in accordance with the Path.
Furthermore, by practicing eighty trillion *pāramitās* over three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, they shall attain the stage of the equal sages and thus abide in the state of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*).

"Furthermore, O Mahāsattva Sujñāta, abiding in the patience of equanimity and practicing the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*), never departing from them in thought after thought, one enters the relinquishment of signlessness (*animitta-upekṣā*). By extinguishing the afflictions of greed within the three realms and being non-dual with the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), one is the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) of the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*); because one extinguishes all signs by taking principle as the object, this is the unconditioned signlessness of cessation through wisdom (*prajñā-pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha-animitta-asaṃskṛta*)."

When abiding in the first stage of patience (*kṣānti*), because the immeasurable future births and deaths are extinguished not by means of cognitive objects, they are not "extinction through non-cognitive conditions" (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). Being signless (*animitta*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), they are devoid of the marks of self and other; and because they are devoid of signs, immeasurable skillful means (*upāya*) all manifest before one.
Regarding the skillful means of contemplating the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*): within the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), one neither sinks nor emerges, neither turns back nor is inverted.
Regarding the skillful means of universal study: one studies everything without either realizing or not realizing.
Regarding the skillful means of dedication: it is neither abiding in the fruit nor not abiding in the fruit, yet one directs oneself toward *sarvajñatā*.
Regarding the skillful means of mastery over Māra: one practices the Buddha-way within what is not the Way, remaining unshakable by the four Māras.
The skillful means of the One Vehicle refers to penetrating all the conduct of sentient beings within the mark of non-duality.
The skillful means of transformation refers to freely manifesting all pure buddha-lands through the power of vows.
Thus it is, son of good family!
This initial awakening-wisdom is non-dual regarding the marks of existence and non-existence; it is the illumination of true wisdom.
Its skillful application—neither realizing nor sinking, neither emerging nor arriving—is the contemplation of expedient means.

For example, water and its waves are neither identical nor different; likewise, because all conditioned phenomena—including the perfections, meditative concentrations, and dhāraṇīs—are neither one nor two, each and every practice is brought to fulfillment.
Because they have practiced the path for four asaṃkhyeya kalpas, they enter this gateway to the treasury of merit.

Since the karmic habits of the three realms no longer arise, they exhaust what is old and do not create what is new; yet, by the power of their vows, they manifest births in all pure lands through transformation.
Because he constantly cultivates the contemplation of equanimity (*upekṣā*), he ascends to the stage of *kumārabhūta* (Crown Prince), and constantly bestows the four great treasures upon others.

Furthermore, the Bodhisattva Guṇamati, by means of the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*), extinguishes the afflictions such as hatred within the three realms of existence; abiding in the stage of Middle Patience (*madhyakṣānti*), he practices all meritorious virtues.

For five asaṃkhyeya kalpas, he practiced the contemplation of great loving-kindness (*maitrī*), such that it was constantly present in every moment of mind; he entered the stage of *animitta-śuddha-pāra* and transformed all sentient beings.

"Furthermore, the practitioner of clear wisdom constantly practices the contemplation of the three insights (trividyā) within the patience of signlessness (animitta-kṣānti). He knows that the dharmas of the three periods of time neither come nor go and have no place of abiding; his mind-moments are quiescently extinguished, and he exhausts the delusions and afflictions of the triple world. Because he attains the contemplation of all merits of the three insights, and because he has accumulated the immeasurable perfection of clarity (vidyā-pāramitā) throughout six asaṃkhyeya kalpas, he enters the stage of Kāraka and maintains all dharmas through the practice of signlessness."

"Furthermore, the Bodhisattva Er-yang Sheng-jue-da, practicing the patience that accords with the Dharma (anulomikī-dharma-kṣānti), turns against the current of the five views, accumulates immeasurable merit, and dwells in the stage of a Srotāpanna."

Constantly possessing the divine eye, divine ear, knowledge of past lives, knowledge of others' minds, and the supernormal power of the body, they extinguish all views of the triple world in every thought-moment; furthermore, having practiced the five supernormal powers for seven asaṃkhyeya kalpas, they never depart from the mind of the pāramitās as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

"Furthermore, the Bodhisattva Supratiṣṭhita, through the patience that accords with the Path (*anulomikī kṣānti*), contemplates by means of the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*) the *nayuta* of internal and external treatises on the Truths, medical prescriptions, crafts, and incantations; therefore, he says: 'I am the Omniscient One.
Because he has extinguished the afflictions such as doubt regarding the three realms, his marks of selfhood (*ātman*) have ceased.
Because he knows that each stage (*bhūmi*) has its point of emergence, it is called the 'Path of Emergence' (*nairyāṇika-mārga*)."
Because there are things that do not yet emerge, it is called "obstructing the Path";
this refers to the doubt regarding the three realms.
Because one cultivates immeasurable merit, one immediately enters the stage of Sakṛdāgāmin.

Furthermore, because they have accumulated the practice of the various *dhāraṇī* gates throughout eight *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, they constantly practice the contemplation of fearlessness (*abhaya-vipaśyanā*) without departing from their minds.

Moreover, they constantly manifest reality by abiding within the stage of *anulomikī-kṣānti* (patience in accordance with truth), performing the contemplation of the Middle Way; because they exhaust all afflictions—the causes of accumulation and the karma of accumulation within the triple world—they contemplate that which is neither existent nor non-existent, as it is a single mark of marklessness and devoid of duality, thereby realizing the stage of *anāgāmin*.
Furthermore, because he accumulated the illumination of the Middle Way for nine asaṃkhyeya kalpas, the power of his joy gives rise to all Buddha-lands.
Moreover, O Bodhisattva Xuanda, those who cultivate the patience of non-arising—the patience of the joy of the Dharma—within ten asaṃkhyeya kalpas, this is called "bondage-patience."
He follows the arising of all paths, yet within the patience of single-mindedness, he extinguishes the habitual causes, karma, and fruits of the triple world.
Abiding in his final body, he fully accomplishes immeasurable merits; the knowledge of non-arising, the knowledge of exhaustion, and the fivefold dharma-body are all perfected.

Abiding in the tenth stage, the rank of the Brahma-Heaven Arhat, he constantly practices the contemplation of the three gates of emptiness; fully endowed with hundreds of thousands of millions of samādhis, he extensively propagates the treasury of the Dharma.

"Furthermore, the Perfectly Awakened One, abiding in the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*), contemplates that the mind and mental objects are quiescent: they are the markless mark, the bodiless body, and the unknowing knowledge. Thus, he employs the mind-vehicle throughout all directions, dwelling in serene detachment within the dwelling of non-dwelling."

While dwelling in existence, one constantly cultivates emptiness; while abiding in emptiness, there are constant myriad transformations. Because one illuminates all dharmas with both [wisdoms], one knows what is possible and what is impossible, and so forth, up to the contemplation of the ten powers of omniscience. Thus, one ascends to the stage of Mahāraga, transforming sentient beings in all lands. For a thousand *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, one practices the dharma of the ten powers, with each thought corresponding to the next, and constantly enters the Samādhi of Seeing the Buddha.

"Furthermore, as for the spiritual transformation of the light of wisdom: abiding in the supreme patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), one extinguishes the characteristics of mind and mental states.
With the Dharma-eye one perceives all phenomena; with the purified three eyes, one perceives that form is empty."
By the power of his great vows, he is constantly born in all pure lands.

Throughout ten thousand *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, he has accumulated the immeasurable Buddha-light samādhi, enabling him to manifest the spiritual powers of as many Buddhas as there are grains of sand in a million Ganges Rivers.
Abiding in the state of the Bhagavat, they also constantly enter the Buddha-flower Samādhi.
Furthermore, regarding the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas who abide in the patience of cessation (kṣānti):

from the time they first resolved their minds until now, having passed through a million asaṃkhyeya kalpas and cultivated merit for a million asaṃkhyeya kalpas, they have ascended to the liberation of all dharmas and dwell upon the Vajra Terrace.
“Good son! From the stage of *kṣānti* (patience) up to the *mūrdhan-samādhi* (summit samādhi), all are termed ‘subduing all afflictions.
Yet, without the conviction of faith, one extinguishes all afflictions and gives rise to the wisdom of liberation;”
Illuminating the ultimate truth (paramārthasatya) is not called "seeing.
What is called "seeing" is omniscience (sarvajñā).
Therefore, from the past until now, I have always said that it is known, seen, and realized only by a Buddha.

From the Samādhi of the Summit (mūrdha-samādhi) down to the stage of Patience through Practice (kṣānti-pratipannaka), that which is not known, not seen, and not realized is understood all at once only by the Buddha; it is not called "faith.

For those who gradually subdue [the afflictions], although wisdom arises and ceases, because they are able to abide in non-arising and non-ceasing, if this mind were to cease, there would be no defilements that would not cease. Through non-arising and non-ceasing, they enter the principle of the ultimate limit, the Vajra-samādhi, which is identical to the true limit (bhūtakoṭi) and equal to the dharma-nature (dharmatā); yet, they have not yet attained equality with the Peerless-Peerless (asamasama).
It is like a person who ascends a high tower and looks down upon all things; there is nothing that is not clearly perceived.
Abiding in the Samādhi of the Exhaustion of Principles is likewise so.
Constantly cultivating all practices to fulfill the treasury of merit, they enter the stage of the Bhagavān and likewise abide eternally in the Buddha-wisdom samādhi. "Good son!

In this way, all these bodhisattvas are able to transform sentient beings within the lands of all Tathāgatas throughout the ten directions, correctly expounding the true meaning, receiving, upholding, reading, and reciting it, and penetrating the reality of suchness, no different from myself today.
The Buddha told King Prasenajit:
"After my parinirvāṇa, when the Dharma is about to perish, you shall uphold this Prajñāpāramitā and perform great buddha-work."
The establishment of all lands and the happiness of the myriad people all arise from this Prajñāpāramitā.
For this reason, it is entrusted to kings, and not entrusted to bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās.
Why is this? Because there is no royal power [to protect it], it has not been entrusted to you.
You should receive, uphold, read, and recite it, and understand its meaning and principles.
"Great King! Of the ten billion Sumeru mountains, ten billion suns and moons, and the four continents within each Sumeru that I have now transformed,
in the southern continent of Jambudvīpa there are sixteen great kingdoms, five hundred intermediate kingdoms, and ten thousand minor kingdoms."

Within that land there are seven calamities; because of these calamities, all kings lecture upon and recite the Prajñāpāramitā. Thereupon, the seven calamities are immediately extinguished and the seven blessings are produced; the myriad subjects live in peace and happiness, and the sovereigns rejoice.
"What are these difficulties?

The sun and moon lose their courses, and the seasons run contrary to their order; sometimes a red sun rises, or a black sun rises, or two, three, four, or five suns rise; sometimes the sun is eclipsed and loses its light, or the solar disc appears with one, two, three, four, or five concentric halos."
When such portents and anomalies occur, one should read and recite this sutra;
this constitutes the first difficulty.

When the twenty-eight lunar mansions lose their proper courses, and when Venus, comets, the wheel-star, the ghost-star, Mars, Mercury, the wind-star, the sword-star, the Southern Dipper, the Northern Dipper, the five great stars of the sacred mountains, all the stars of national rulers, the stars of the Three Dukes, and the stars of the hundred officials—when all such stars manifest various portents—one should likewise read and recite this sutra.
This constitutes two difficulties.

When a great fire burns the kingdom and the myriad people are consumed, whether it be fires from ghosts, dragons, heavens, mountain deities, humans, trees, or bandits—amidst such strange portents—one should likewise read and recite this sutra.
These are the three calamities. When great floods submerge the populace;

when the seasons run contrary to their course, with rain in winter and snow in summer; when there is thunder, lightning, and peals of thunder in winter; when ice, frost, hail, and sleet fall in the sixth month; when red water, black water, and blue water rain down; when earth-mountains, stone-mountains, sand, gravel, and rocks rain down; when rivers flow upstream, carrying mountains afloat and stones adrift—when such transformations occur, one should likewise read and recite this sutra.
This constitutes the fourth difficulty.

When great winds blow and kill the myriad people, and when the lands, mountains, rivers, and trees are all suddenly submerged and destroyed—during such times of calamitous winds, black winds, red winds, blue winds, celestial winds, terrestrial winds, and fire-winds—one should likewise recite this sutra.
This constitutes the fifth difficulty.

When heaven and earth, the lands, and the territories are scorched by intense heat and blazing fires; when the hundred grasses wither from drought and the five grains fail to ripen; when the soil is set ablaze and the myriad people perish—during such times of transformation, one should likewise read this sutra.
These constitute the six hardships.

When enemies from the four quarters come to invade, when rebels arise within and without the realm, when there are calamities of fire, water, wind, or spirits, when the common people fall into chaos, and when the kalpa of weapons arises—during such extraordinary times as these, one should also read this sutra.
This constitutes the seventh peril. "Great King!
This Prajñāpāramitā is the divine root of the mind-consciousness of all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and all sentient beings; it is the father and mother of all kings."
It is also called the Divine Talisman, the Ghost-Repelling Pearl, the Wish-Fulfilling Pearl, the Nation-Protecting Pearl, the Heaven-and-Earth Mirror, and the Dragon-Treasure King.
The Buddha told the Great King:
"You should prepare banners of nine colors, nine zhang in length;
and flowers of nine colors, two zhang in height."
There were thousand-branched lamps, five *zhang* in height;
nine jade caskets and nine jade cloths, as well as tables made of the seven treasures, upon which the sutra was placed.

Whenever the king traveled, [the attendants] would always keep it a full hundred paces ahead of him. This sutra constantly emitted a thousand rays of light, ensuring that within a thousand *li*, the seven calamities did not arise and transgressions were not produced.

When the king resides there, he shall construct a canopy of the seven precious gems, within which is a high seat of the seven precious gems; upon this he shall place the scripture scrolls, making offerings to them day after day by scattering flowers and burning incense, as if serving his parents or serving Śakra, the Lord of Devas.
"Great King!
I now see clearly with my five eyes that all kings of the three periods of time have become sovereign rulers because they served five hundred Buddhas in their past lives;
for this reason, all holy ones and arhats come to be born in those kingdoms to bring about great benefit."
When a king’s merit is exhausted, all holy persons will abandon him.
When all holy persons have departed, the seven calamities will inevitably arise.
"Great King! [he said.]
If in future ages there are kings who protect and uphold the Triple Gem, I shall dispatch five Bodhisattvas of Great Power to guard their kingdoms:
first, Vajraghoṣa Bodhisattva, who will go to guard that kingdom holding a thousand-jeweled wheel;
second, Nāgarājaghoṣa Bodhisattva, who will go to guard that kingdom holding a golden wheel-lamp.
Third, the Bodhisattva Fearless Ten-Power Roar held a vajra in his hand and went to protect that land;
fourth, the Bodhisattva Thunder-and-Lightning Roar held a net of a thousand jewels in his hand and went to protect that land;
fifth, the Bodhisattva Infinite Power Roar held five thousand sword-wheels in his hand and went to protect that land.
"The five great beings and five thousand great divine kings will bring great benefit to your kingdom; you should fashion their images and make offerings to them.
"Great King! [he continued].
I now entrust the Three Jewels to you, all you kings:

those of the kingdoms of Kośala, Śrāvastī, Magadha, Vārāṇasī, Kāśī, Kauśāmbī, Kauśala, Kuru, Vatsa, Mithilā, Karakaṇḍu, Gandhāra, Sādhū, Saṃghāṭa, Kaṃcanapūrva, and Pāṭaliputra. All such kings as these should receive, uphold, and practice the Prajñāpāramitā.
At that time, the great assembly and the asura kings, hearing the Buddha speak of the seven terrors of future ages, their hair stood on end, and they cried out in a loud voice, saying:
"May we never be born in that land!"

At that time, the sixteen great kings entrusted the affairs of state to their younger brothers, left the household life to practice the Way, and contemplated the characteristics of the four great elements and the four colors as being transcendent. They contemplated the characteristics of the non-appropriation of the four great elements and four colors through consciousness-emptiness-entry-practice, the characteristics of the thirty patiences and the first stage (*bhūmi*), and the characteristics of the nine stages of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
Therefore, Great King, you shall cast off the body of an ordinary person and enter the body of the sixth stage;
you shall cast off the body of the sevenfold retribution and enter the eighth dharma-body, realizing the *prajñāpāramitā* of all practices.

The eighteen Brahmā heavens and the asura kings attained the contemplation of the three vehicles as being identical to the realm of non-arising; they further scattered flowers in offering: flowers of emptiness, flowers of the dharma-nature, flowers of the sages, flowers of compliance, flowers of non-arising, flowers of dharma-joy, vajra flowers, flowers of the middle way through the contemplation of conditions, and flowers of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, scattering them upon the Buddha and the assembly of nine hundred billion great bodhisattvas.

All the others who had realized the traces and fruits of the Path scattered flowers of the empty mind, flowers of the tree of the mind, flowers of the six pāramitās, and flowers of wondrous enlightenment over the Buddha and the entire assembly.

Ten thousand bodhisattvas, mindful of sentient beings in future ages, immediately realized the Samādhi of Wondrous Enlightenment, the Samādhi of Perfect Clarity, the Vajra Samādhi, the Samādhi of Worldly Truth, the Samādhi of Ultimate Truth, and the Samādhi of the Supreme Truth—these three samādhis of truth are the King of All Samādhis—and they also attained the Immeasurable Samādhi, the Seven Treasures Samādhi, the Twenty-five Existences Samādhi, and the Samādhi of All Practices.
Furthermore, ten billion bodhisattvas ascended to the Vajra-Pinnacle and manifested perfect enlightenment. **Chapter Eight:
Entrustment** *The Benevolent Kings’ Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra for the Protection of the State* The Buddha addressed King Prasenajit: “I exhort you all:

after my parinirvāṇa, during the periods of eighty years, eight hundred years, or eight thousand years when there is no Buddha, no Dharma, and no Saṃgha; when there are no faithful men and no faithful women—at that time, I entrust this sūtra and the Three Jewels to the various kings and the fourfold assembly of disciples to uphold, recite, and explain its meaning. For the sake of sentient beings within the three realms, you shall open the path of wisdom of emptiness, cultivate the seven practices of the worthy and the ten virtuous deeds, and transform all sentient beings.”

In the future age of the five turbidities, the fourfold assembly of bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, the eight classes of devas and nāgas, all the divine kings, as well as kings, ministers, crown princes, and sons of kings, will, relying on their own nobility and high status, destroy and subvert my Dharma.
I shall now establish a restrictive rule for my disciples, the bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs:
they are not permitted to leave the household life or practice the Path, nor are they permitted to fashion images of the Buddha or stupas of the Buddha.
They established an official system for the clergy and required monks to register their names;
they mandated that bhikṣus stand on the ground while laypeople sat on high seats;
and they permitted soldiers and slaves to become bhikṣus.
Regarding the method for accepting special invitations:

if a bhikṣu forms a close and intimate bond with a lay acquaintance and, for the sake of seeking merit, performs a vegetarian feast on their behalf, this is entirely according to the methods of non-Buddhists and is not our Dharma at all.
"You should know that at that time, the True Dharma will not long remain before it perishes.
Great King!
It is you who have brought about the ruin and disorder of my Way."
Relying on their own power and might, they have suppressed my fourfold assembly of disciples.

The common people suffer from diseases and hardships without exception; this is the cause for the ruin of the nation, and the sins of the five turbidities could not be fully described even in an entire kalpa.
“Great King!

In the final age of the Dharma, there will be bhikṣus among the fourfold assembly of disciples, and kings and ministers will frequently engage in unrighteous conduct, arbitrarily committing great acts of unrighteousness against the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṃgha, and committing various transgressions that are contrary to the Dharma and the Vinaya, binding bhikṣus like common prisoners in a jail.”
"At that time, the Dharma will not have long remained before it perishes. Great King!

After my parinirvāṇa, in future ages, the fourfold assembly of disciples—including minor kings, crown princes, and sons of kings—who were originally those who maintained and protected the Triple Gem, will instead further destroy and disperse the Triple Gem."
It is like the worms within a lion’s body that eat the lion itself; they are not external parasites.

Many will destroy my Buddha-dharma, incurring great transgressions. As the true teaching declines and thins, the people will lack correct conduct; they will gradually turn toward evil, and their lifespan will diminish day by day until it reaches only one hundred years.

When people destroy the Buddha's teachings, there will no longer be filial sons; the six kin will live in discord, and the celestial deities will offer no protection. Epidemics and malevolent spirits will come daily to inflict harm, with calamities and portents following one another in succession and misfortunes spreading in all directions. Upon death, they will enter the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals;

if they emerge again as humans, they will receive the retribution of being soldiers or slaves—just as an echo responds to a sound, or as characters remain visible even when the lamp is extinguished after writing at night.
The retributions of the three realms are likewise thus.
"Great King!

In future ages, all kings, crown princes, sons of kings, and the fourfold assembly of disciples will arbitrarily impose written codes and prohibitions upon my disciples, following the laws for laypeople or the laws for soldiers and slaves. If my disciples—whether bhikṣus or bhikṣuṇīs—are required to register their names and be conscripted by the government, they are no longer my disciples at all; this is the law of soldiers and slaves."

The Office of the Head of the Sangha (Lìtǒngguān) oversees the monastic codes and manages the registers of monks; the Great and Small Sangha Heads together exercise mutual control over one another, like the laws for prisoners in jail or for soldiers and slaves.
At that time, the Buddha-dharma will not endure for long.
"Great King!

In future ages, various minor kings and their fourfold assemblies of disciples will themselves create the causes and conditions for this sin that destroys their kingdoms; they alone shall suffer the consequences, and it is not the fault of the Buddha, the Dharma, or the Sangha."
"Great King!
In future ages, this sutra shall circulate; it is the vessel for the Dharma of the seven Buddhas and the path constantly traversed by the Buddhas of the ten directions.

Yet there will be many evil bhikṣus who, seeking fame and profit, shall speak before kings, crown princes, and sons of kings about the causes and conditions for the destruction of the Buddha-dharma and the causes and conditions for the ruin of the nation."

If that king does not discern the truth but believes and listens to these words, he will arbitrarily establish laws and regulations that do not rely on the Buddha’s precepts; this constitutes the causal conditions for destroying the Buddha and destroying the nation.
At such a time, the True Dharma will not endure for long.

At that time, the sixteen great kings, having heard the Buddha’s exposition on future events within the Seven Admonitions, wept with tears streaming down their faces; their cries shook the trichiliocosm, causing the sun, moon, five planets, and twenty-eight lunar mansions to lose their radiance and vanish from sight.

At that time, the various kings each received and upheld the Buddha’s words with a sincere heart, resolving not to obstruct the fourfold assembly of disciples from leaving home to practice the Way, but rather to act in accordance with the Buddha’s teachings.
At that time, the great assembly—the eighteen Brahma kings and the various devaputras of the six heavens of desire—exclaimed:
"At such a time as this, the world is empty and void; it is an age without a Buddha!"

At that time, within the immeasurable great assembly—consisting of ten billion bodhisattvas such as Maitreya, Siṃhacandra, and others; ten billion Śāriputras, Subhūtis, and others; five hundred billion Brahmā kings of the eighteen heavens and the various devas of the six heavens of the desire realm; and the kings of the asuras from the three realms and the six paths of existence—hearing the Buddha’s exposition on the causes and conditions for protecting the fruit of buddhahood and the causes and conditions for protecting the land, they were filled with immeasurable joy. They prostrated before the Buddha and received and upheld the Prajñāpāramitā.
